extracted.intended_audience: students/scholars of humor theory, playwrights, and performers studying the mechanics of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying theoretical principles that explain why situations, words, gestures, and characters provoke laughter; aimed at analyzing or creating comic effects in drama, prose, and performance. Emphasisesmechanical vs. living contrasts, repetition, suggestion, and transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Something mechanical encrusted upon the living
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental comic image: a mechanical or artificial element imposed on something living (the human body or person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This single central image yields many comic effects as it is transferred to subtler spheres (e.g., administrative formality replacing moral law, ready-made garments vs. living body). Treating the living as if it were a machine (rigidity, automatism) produces laughter; examples include garments substituted for a body and administrative enactments standing in for moral laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical intrusion when the moral is expected
rubrics_metrics.description: An occurrence is comic when attention is suddenly shifted from the soul/moral/intellectual side to the physical/material side of a person in a context where the moral is pertinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic examples: a speaker sneezing at a pathetic moment, the phrase 'He was virtuous and plump.' In tragedy, any reminder of bodily needs (eating, sitting) risks turning the scene comic. The more the body’s demands are petty and monotonously repeated, the stronger the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner triumphing over matter (form replaces substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arises when outward form, procedure, or professional etiquette is pursued at the expense of real ends or substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ridicule of professions (lawyers, doctors, magistrates) where scrupulous observance of form becomes an end in itself. Quoted comic aphorisms (e.g., 'You are only bound to treat people according to form') illustrate how means supplant ends; this professional automatism is laughable. Use examples from stage characters who prioritize form over function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubling of ridicule: physical defect as overtone to professional folly
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic 'note' (e.g., appearance seeking to triumph over reality) is naturally accompanied by overtones such as physical defects that complete the professional ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/actors often duplicate a professional absurdity with a matching physical peculiarity (stammering judge preparing us to see intellectual ossification). If the author omits a physical defect, performers will often invent one to complete the effect (examples: Molière's ridiculous doctors with contrasting speech rhythms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Person perceived as a thing
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh when a person gives the impression of being a thing—when human qualities are reduced to inert, mechanical, or object-like attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: circus clowns evolving visually into balls or dummies, Sancho Panza tossed like a quilt, Munchausen as a cannon-ball. Comic staging/acting that progressively dehumanizes figures (rounding forms, increased rigidity) evokes this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion / solidification (vague → distinct)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of producing comic hallucination by slowly transforming an initially vague, fluid impression into a distinct, concrete, and absurd image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to hypnotic suggestion: start from perceived objects and make perception more indefinite, then gradually bring out the absurd image. Techniques include rhythmic and repetitive patterns (rhythm, rhyme, assonance) that lull the imagination into accepting the suggested vision. Literary examples: catalogues or lists whose piling-up of like terms suggest a doll/thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition as mechanical spring (Jack‑in‑the‑box)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition on stage is comic when it symbolizes a mechanical spring: a repressed feeling that bursts out, is checked, and bursts out again, producing an automatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Childish games (Jack‑in‑the‑box) and Punch-and-Judy rhythms illustrate how repeated blows/returns escalate laughter. Repetition of words or actions is not inherently funny; it is laughable when it signals a recurrent, repressed impulse (examples: Dorine/Orgon 'Et Tartuffe?', Harpagon's 'No dowry wanted!').

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner duality / mechanical oscillation within a character
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations are comic when a single character contains opposing, inelastic impulses (e.g., truth-telling vs politeness) that oscillate mechanically, making the scene effectively an inner duel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic often occurs not between two persons but within one (e.g., Alceste repeating 'I don't say that!'), where each repetition reveals the struggle between two parts of the self. Make the oscillation habitual/mechanical to convert seriousness into comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad comic situation: life + mechanical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any arrangement of acts and events is broadly comic which simultaneously gives the illusion of life and the distinct impression of a mechanical contrivance operating within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle links adult comedy to childhood games (puppets, strings). When characters seem alive yet move or behave according to mechanical rules, the contrast produces laughter. Use simplified, magnified theatrical situations to reveal this dual impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative extension and progressive continuity of comic images
rubrics_metrics.description: Many comic forms become comic by resemblance to another comic image, with the comic impression gliding by analogy from one image to another, often into remote and multiple analogies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic fancy is a living energy that spreads and subdivides (like branches of a tree), so analysis must follow the chain of associations back to the starting point. This explains why some comic effects only make sense given their relation to other, earlier comic images.
